name: Classical Hollywood
summary: A studio craft in which the camera, the light and the cut serve a clear story. Three-point light, a master shot with coverage and a smooth match cut. The style hides itself.

philosophy.core_thesis: A film serves its story, so every device (light, angle, cut and score) is invisible and keeps the viewer's eye on the character and the action.
design_principles: Light each face with a three-point setup at a key-to-fill ratio of 3:1 to 4:1, a back light at 1.5 to 2 times the key and a soft eye light.
Shoot a master shot and cover each scene with a medium shot and a close-up from 3 to 5 set-ups, and keep the 180° line.
Cut for continuity on action, at an average shot length of 8 to 12 s, with the match cut hidden inside a movement.
Frame in 1.37:1 (1.33:1 to 1.37:1) at eye level, a 40mm to 75mm lens, with the star in a medium close-up in the centre third.
Use a dolly or a crane move of 0.3 to 0.8 m/s only to follow a character, and finish it on a stop.
Score under the scene with a leitmotif per character at −18 to −22 dB below the dialogue, and a rising cue before an act break.
Resolve the plot in three acts of 25%, 50% and 25% of the runtime and end on a closed, legible image.
anti_patterns: A jump cut that shows the edit
A handheld shake with no motive
An open ending with no resolution
A camera that looks into the lens
A shot that breaks the 180° line without a reason
A location sound track with unclear dialogue

composition.framing: A 1.37:1 frame at eye level with the star in the centre third; head room of 5% to 10% and a balanced two-shot.
composition.staging_in_depth: A foreground of 1 to 2 m, a middle of the actors and a back plane lit apart from them; the background is soft or lit lower.
composition.subject_placement: The star on a third line, facing 3/4 to the lens, and the other actor in the opposite third.

principles.rule: Light each face with a key, a fill and a back light so that the figure separates from the set.
principles.value: 3:1 to 4:1 key to fill, back light 1.5× key

principles.rule: Give the star the brightest and sharpest mass of the frame, in a medium close-up.
principles.value: star on a third, 40% to 60% of the frame height

principles.rule: Keep the eyelines and the 180° line stable across a scene so that the viewer always knows who looks at whom.
principles.value: 1 line of action per scene, 0 crossings

principles.rule: Place the eyes on the upper third line and balance a two-shot on both thirds.
Balance a lit star on one side with a darker mass or a prop on the other.

camera_and_movement.movement: A smooth dolly or crane move, motivated by a character, and ended on a stop. The pan follows the action and leads it by a little.
camera_and_movement.support: Studio dolly, crane and tripod with a geared head
camera_and_movement.camera_height: 1.2 to 1.7 m, eye level; low for a villain, rarely above 2 m
camera_and_movement.move_speed: Dolly 0.3 to 0.8 m/s; pan 10° to 25° per second

lens_and_format.focal_length: 40mm to 75mm (35mm format); 25mm to 35mm for deep-focus sets
lens_and_format.aperture: f/2.8 to f/5.6 with a soft background; f/8 for deep focus
lens_and_format.focus: Selective focus on the star; a diffusion filter on the close-up of a woman.

light.quality: Soft on faces through diffusion, hard on the set and hair; glamour light with a clean modelling shadow.
light.direction: Key at 45° and above eye level, fill from the camera side, a back light from above and behind.
light.key_to_fill_ratio: 3:1 to 4:1 (1.6 to 2 stops); 8:1 for film noir
light.colour_temperature: Tungsten 3200K, with Technicolor balanced to 3200K at high light levels
light.source: Studio arcs, tungsten and a soft eye light

colour_and_grade.treatment: Rich black and white with a full tonal range, or three-strip Technicolor with saturated primaries and warm skin.
grade_recipe: Set the black point at 2% and the white point at 97% for a full-range print.
Apply a medium S-curve of +20% contrast and a soft shoulder in the highlights.
For colour, push red and blue saturation by +25% and warm the skin to 5% to 8% magenta-yellow.
Add a diffusion glow of 5% to 10% on the highlights of a close-up.
Keep grain at 6% to 10%; no vignette and no teal cast.
colour_and_grade.texture: Fine grain at 6% to 10%, clean blacks and a glow on the highlights

editing_and_rhythm.average_shot_length: 8 to 12 s for the 1930s and 1940s (estimate from Salt and Cinemetrics; check each title)
editing_and_rhythm.shot_length_range: 1.5 s for an insert to 40 s for a long dialogue take
editing_and_rhythm.cutting_logic: Cut on the action and on the eyeline so that the viewer does not see the edit. Start a scene wide, go to medium and then to the close-up on the key line.
editing_and_rhythm.transitions: Hard cut on action, a dissolve of 1 to 2 s for a time jump, a fade to black of 1 s at an act, a wipe for a montage.

sound.approach: Clean studio dialogue, a scored track and foley added in post; the room is silent.
sound.dialogue: Clear and quick, with sharp diction and no overlap, at a steady rate of 160 to 200 words per minute.
sound.music: A full orchestral score with a leitmotif for each character, under the dialogue and swelling at the act break.
sound.loudness: −23 LUFS integrated for a restoration, dialogue at −12 dBFS average

titles_and_graphics.treatment: A big title sequence on a painted or a live backdrop, with cast cards; the studio logo and the credits come before the story.
titles_and_graphics.type: A bold serif or a script in the title, a plain serif in the credits, 3 to 6 s per card, white on a painted ground.

shot_primer.opening: Open on an establishing shot of a place, with a title or a pan that lands on the lead; hold 4 to 6 s.

emotion.target_response: Comfort and absorption: the viewer follows the story and the stars without noticing the craft.

use_cases: video prompts for a studio-era scene
title sequences with a glamour tone
avoid_when: The brief needs an observed, unplanned reality.
The piece must feel raw, current or amateur.

modifiers.how: Keep the black and white and the 1.37:1 frame; leave the studio for a street, drop the glamour key and use daylight with a bounce.
Keep the studio and the black and white; raise the key-to-fill ratio to 8:1 and let a shadow take 40% or more of the frame.

sources.title: Wikidata Q309153: Singin' in the Rain
David Bordwell, Janet Staiger and Kristin Thompson, The Classical Hollywood Cinema (Columbia University Press, 1985)
Barry Salt, Film Style and Technology: History and Analysis (Starword, 3rd ed., 2009)
